correspondence.component_scope: Western opening and first northeastward turn
correspondence.finding: The western beginning and its first northeastward rise are in the southern Inland Ice, inland of the southeastern coastal mountains. This western opening extends beyond the regional Skjoldungen sheet. The retained national original covers it continuously and overlaps the regional map farther east. No river label or mapped natural river follows this selected ice-interior opening.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern ice-interior arc and eastward crest
correspondence.finding: The long northern/eastward portion near 64°N remains in the mapped Inland Ice. It runs through the western marginal area of Sheet 14 before turning southeast. The original national map shows ice-surface contours, ice-thickness isopachs and below-ice bedrock contours in this region; these are distinct legend symbols, not river channels. The regional original confirms broad continuous ice terrain, not hydraulic continuity along the model line.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Long southeastward diagonal into the lower ice-margin belt
correspondence.finding: The long diagonal runs southeast through the inland ice toward the coastal ice/nunatak belt. Regional original pixels cover the full diagonal and its southern bend, including the ice west of the Gyldenbørste nunatak area. Nearby exposed-rock islands and mountain belts are distinguished from the pale-blue ice. The selected model is not promoted to a surveyed glacier centreline, surface channel or subglacial drainage path.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward lower approach south of the Thrym Gletscher sector
correspondence.finding: The eastward run lies in the ice/rock corridor around and south of the Gyldenbørste area, west and south of the mapped Thrym Gletscher sector. The source shows ice threaded among exposed nunataks and the headward coastal rock belt. The nearby Thrym Gletscher and Graah Fjord labels identify neighbouring glacier/fjord geography; neither is a river name for this selected object. Blue stippling is the source’s undifferentiated Quaternary-cover symbol, not proof of a lake link.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Southeastward bend into the Skinfaxe sector
correspondence.finding: The subsequent southeastward/southward bend occupies the mapped ice-and-nunatak approach to Skinfaxe, immediately west of the western Skjoldungen coastal rock/fjord belt. Skinfaxe is printed across ice terrain; the adjacent Rimfaxe, Guldfaxe and Kong Faxe labels belong to distinct neighbouring ice corridors. The selected route is considered through the actual mapped ice/rock transitions at ordinary generalized scale, without assigning every model segment to one glacier or claiming that it is a continuous natural river.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual ending in the Skinfaxe–inner Kangertoq setting
correspondence.finding: The final southeastward and southward pieces reach the historical mapped Skinfaxe–inner Kangertoq ice/fjord-head sector. The source distinguishes the pale-blue glacier corridor, adjacent coloured rock and the white fjord water. Kangertoq is a contextual fjord label, not a river hydronym. The actual endpoint is not relocated to Skjoldungen, Graah Fjord, Sehested Fjord or another nearby name. This is a generalized terminal-setting correspondence, not a surveyed present ice-front, exact shoreline crossing or confirmation of an ordinary river mouth.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Whole selected feature, branch/lake scope and feature identity
correspondence.finding: All selected geometry is accounted for from interior ice to the southeastern ice/rock/fjord-head setting. The selected object contains one retained mainstem FID; no separately selected tributary geometry requires a river-branch name. No material through-lake or reservoir connector is established or missing in this selected corridor, and neighbouring rock/cover symbols are not turned into lakes. The maps do not establish one natural-river hydronym or surface/subglacial hydraulic continuity across the full modelled route. Full terrain correspondence therefore ends in a completed name-scope hold.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete selected terrain correspondence; no continuous natural-river identity or hydraulic continuity inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: colorado headward opening
correspondence.finding: The western opening lies in gently dissected uplands in the Cheyenne–Kiowa county setting, west of US 385. The maps show unnamed intermittent branches tending southeast and then east across the county boundary. No source read establishes a name or the entire selected westernmost opening.
correspondence.correspondence: Headward terrain and nearby channel pattern read; selected full opening not established.

correspondence.component_scope: colorado unnamed channels and depressions
correspondence.finding: East of US 385 the initial unnamed channel reaches a wetland/depression setting. The selected route continues southeast into another east-trending intermittent-channel corridor, passes a small pond/depression setting and turns northeast toward South Fork White Woman Creek. The original cartography shows these local channels, wetland symbols and ponds, but does not show the full selected transfers between them or a continuous through-link to the South Fork.
correspondence.correspondence: All selected western corridor settings inspected in overlapping originals; material through-connections unresolved.

correspondence.component_scope: south fork and main creek junction
correspondence.finding: The selected downstream Colorado–Kansas border reach follows the mapped South Fork White Woman Creek, which joins the separately mapped White Woman Creek in western Greeley County. The selection then follows White Woman Creek southeast. The South Fork's independently mapped upper channel is not a justification for naming the selected earlier unnamed route after it.
correspondence.correspondence: Named border reach and main-creek junction established at generalized corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: greeley county trunk
correspondence.finding: The selected main corridor follows White Woman Creek across Greeley County, passing the Tribune area and continuing east toward Wichita County. Original cartography shows a sinuous intermittent creek with tributary junctions and no major lake or reservoir passage on this selected reach.

correspondence.component_scope: wichita county trunk
correspondence.finding: The route continues through Wichita County, crosses the Highway 96 corridor west of Leoti, passes south of Leoti and continues southeast toward Scott County. Sand Creek is separately mapped to its south. KGS describes the White Woman and Sand Creek system as intermittent; that historical account is not a present-day flow measurement.

correspondence.component_scope: sand creek junction and lower bend
correspondence.finding: Sand Creek joins White Woman Creek just inside Scott County from the south. The selected lower route continues east and then turns northeast. This is the White Woman trunk receiving Sand Creek, rather than a selection of Sand Creek's upstream course.
correspondence.correspondence: Material junction and lower change of direction established.

correspondence.component_scope: scott basin terminal
correspondence.finding: The lower creek approaches the broad low-relief basin south of Scott City and runs northeast toward the US 83 corridor, where the mapped drainage attenuates in the depression. KGS expressly identifies its receiving setting as the Scott Basin southeast of Scott City. The mapped terminal is a basin/depression setting, not a mapped confluence with a larger river or a named lake/reservoir passage.
correspondence.correspondence: Actual generalized receiving/terminal setting established independently of the retained model terminal class.
correspondence.limits: No exact ending point, permanent-water extent, current discharge or event-specific overflow claim.

correspondence.component_scope: Initial northward opening and northern turn west of Bruni
correspondence.finding: The selected line begins in ranch and low-relief terrain, proceeds north past small isolated water patches and the highway setting west of Bruni, and turns east toward Arroyo de los Angeles. The original headward map shows roads, contours, scattered tanks or ponds, and a distinct channel farther east, but does not establish the entire selected initial northward and eastward route as a continuous waterway. The northern loop is not assigned the Arroyo de los Angeles name merely because it eventually approaches that mapped drainage.

correspondence.component_scope: Arroyo de los Angeles corridor beside Bruni
correspondence.finding: After the unresolved western opening, the selected eastward and southeastward corridor corresponds at generalized scale to the mapped Arroyo de los Angeles near Bruni. It crosses the Webb–Duval county setting and continues toward the northern Hebbronville approach. Mapped tributary approaches from north and southwest remain separate; the selected line is not extended to all of their sources.

correspondence.component_scope: Mesquite Creek and Noriacitas Creek junction at Hebbronville
correspondence.finding: The overlapping maps carry the selected southern approach into the Mesquite Creek corridor east of Hebbronville, across the Highway359 and Highway285 settings. The Noriacitas Creek approach from the west joins this drainage; downstream cartography labels the eastward trunk Palo Blanco Creek. Noriacitas Creek is junction context rather than the selected upstream route. The Arroyo de los Angeles, Mesquite Creek and Palo Blanco labels are not treated as one uniform whole-feature hydronym.

correspondence.component_scope: Western and middle Palo Blanco Creek to Falfurrias
correspondence.finding: The selected line follows the mapped intermittent Palo Blanco Creek east through the Jim Hogg–Brooks setting south of Highway285, turns through the broad southward bend, and continues northeast and east to Falfurrias. Laborcitas Creek approaches from the north and joins west of Falfurrias. The overlapping original views establish the full selected middle corridor at ordinary scale; nearby stock-water bodies and tributaries do not become unnamed gaps or change the trunk name.

correspondence.component_scope: Falfurrias, Cibolo junction and inlet to inland Laguna Salada
correspondence.finding: Original cartography shows the selected Palo Blanco route passing the Falfurrias and Highway281 setting, receiving the Cibolo Creek approach, turning south beside the airport area, and entering the inland Laguna Salada. Arroyo Baluarte and the Una de Gato drainage approach from the west/southwest into the lake-entry setting. These are distinct tributary junctions. The selected lake passage is generalized through the northern lake/inlet/outlet setting and does not imply exact bank agreement.

correspondence.component_scope: Inland Laguna Salada outlet and Palo Blanco Creek to Cayo Lake
correspondence.finding: The map distinguishes inland Laguna Salada from the northern Los Olmos drainage. Palo Blanco Creek continues east from the inland lake through an intermittent-channel and small-waterbody corridor into Cayo Lake southwest of Sarita. The selected line corresponds to this corridor and the Cayo Lake setting at generalized scale. The lake has a curved northeastern extension; the selected onward eastward transfer requires separate evidence. No material named reservoir passage is established along this selected reach.

correspondence.component_scope: Selected Cayo Lake–Sarita–coastal creek transfer
correspondence.finding: The selected line continues east and northeast away from the Cayo Lake setting, crosses the highway south of Sarita, and proceeds through ranch, low-relief woodland and scattered water patches toward a north-trending coastal creek. The original maps do not show a continuous selected waterway through this broad interval. The GLO report supplies a generalized regional stream-network figure, but does not separately establish this material lake-to-coast transfer. A basin boundary, named stream label elsewhere, or continuous model line does not close the missing connection. This is not a claim that all flood or subsurface connections are impossible.

correspondence.component_scope: Final north-trending wetland creek and actual Baffin Bay endpoint
correspondence.finding: The last selected northern reach corresponds at generalized scale to a mapped unnamed creek and wetland inlet reaching the southern shore of Baffin Bay south of La Parra Landing. The retained line ends just into that mapped bay setting. Its creek name remains unestablished in the inspected originals. The coastal Laguna Salada arm lies to the north and receives Los Olmos Creek; it is distinct from inland Laguna Salada near Falfurrias and is not the selected final mouth. The terminal finding comes from the original map and regional bay figure, not from the retained sea metadata. It does not establish the unresolved Cayo Lake-to-coast connection or a natural mouth point for one continuous named river.
correspondence.terminal_setting: Baffin Bay, south of La Parra Landing

correspondence.component_scope: Extreme eastern opening on the western Cordillera Domeyko flank
correspondence.finding: The selected beginning lies in the northern Chaco headward setting north of Cerro Dos Hermanos and Cerro del Chaco. MMA and IGM identify the downstream westward branch as Chaco Norte. The historical IGN original depicts the corresponding intermittent valley and Aguada Ojo del Chaco farther west, but its drawn channel and the finer agency linework all end short of the complete selected eastern extension. Terrain/basin setting alone is not used to invent that first channel connection. The selected starting vertex is not declared a natural or official source.

correspondence.component_scope: Chaco Norte westward branch and southern joining ravines
correspondence.finding: West of the unresolved extreme opening, the selected line follows the mapped Chaco Norte branch through its westward course. The original MMA overview shows the Chaco Sur approach joining from the southeast; farther west the distinct Incaguasi approach joins from the south and the receiving valley is labeled Quebrada del Chaco. IGN independently depicts the Chaco valley, Ojo del Chaco, and the separate Incahuasi setting. The selection does not ascend Chaco Sur or Incaguasi and does not follow the separate Río Frío drainage east of the range.

correspondence.component_scope: Chaco approach to the middle alluvial-fan corridor
correspondence.finding: The selected corridor continues west through the Chaco valley, north of San Venancio and then into the broad intermontane fan country. The original MMA and IGM layers separately depict San Venancio and the Corcovado/Blanca Lidia drainage to the south, with Sandon and Vaquillas north of the Chaco approach. The historical IGN original supplies the terrain, intermittent-channel and road/locality context; the mapped aguadas are not represented as broad lake surfaces.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern middle-fan excursion and southwestward return
correspondence.finding: Within the fan east of Agua Verde, the selection departs the finer mapped Chaco line, crosses toward an adjacent northern strand and then returns southwest through the converging fan network. IGM and MMA depict distinct nearby branches rather than the complete selected inter-strand transfer. IGN 1:500,000 positively locates the broad Chaco dry-valley/fan setting but is too generalized to settle this transfer. The planning basin map supplies regional context only. No inspected primary source establishes the entire selected connection; this is not converted into a completed name-only hold or a claim that no drainage can occur across the fan.

correspondence.component_scope: Agua Verde and western Taltal receiving valley
correspondence.finding: West of the fan, the selected corridor converges toward Agua Verde and follows the repeatedly labeled Quebrada Taltal westward. The historical original shows the receiving valley through the Agua Verde, Los Ratones, Canchas and Breas surroundings, while MMA depicts the corresponding branch convergence and long westward then southwestward course. The separately approaching San Venancio/Corcovado system and the northern Sandon/Vaquillas network remain tributary context. Source line differences do not define exact name-transition boundaries.

correspondence.component_scope: Breas turn, Peineta junction and northwestern city approach
correspondence.finding: The selected western bend reaches the Breas/La Peineta junction setting and turns northwest toward Taltal. IGM labels the eastern selected valley Q. Taltal and the separate south-eastern joining valley Q. de la Peineta; the model does not continue upstream into Peineta. Historical IGN places the connection beside Breas and the La Quinta approach. The planning report separately identifies Cortaderas and Tipias as lower tributaries and describes the receiving Taltal valley toward the urban fan. No name is assigned to every small unnamed lower branch.

correspondence.component_scope: Taltal urban alluvial fan and actual selected coastal terminal
correspondence.finding: The selected final course approaches the city of Taltal from the southeast, crosses the coastal fan/urban setting and ends in the immediate bay water off Taltal on the Pacific coast. IGN depicts the Taltal coast and lower ravine destination; COT maps the landward coastal boundary and urban/industrial patch; the planning original distinguishes the city fan and the Pacific and places Taltal drainage at the city. The final straight modeled extension is not adopted as a current surveyed channel or engineered outfall. The northern San Ramón drainage and southern Los Zanjones/Cifuncho routes are separate, not substitute terminals.

correspondence.component_scope: Waterbody and dry-channel scope across the selection
correspondence.finding: No major selected lake, reservoir or salt-flat crossing is depicted by the inspected original corridor maps. Historical spring/aguada symbols at Ojo del Chaco and other valley settings are distinct from lake interiors. The planning source describes Chaco and Taltal as intermittently activated dry drainage, and explains loss of surface water into the porous interior fan. This is bounded historical/cartographic evidence, not a present wetness or groundwater-operation determination.
